scenes.tts: Take a young kitten. Close one eye for six days. Then record from cells in its visual cortex, one at a time. The closed eye can now drive only a fraction of the cells it drove before. Now close both eyes instead. The harm is far smaller. Why would two closed eyes do less harm than one?
scenes.visual: kitten, eye closes, electrode on a cortex cell, cells shift to the open eye; both eyes close and cells stay mixed; question mark
scenes.narration: Take a young kitten. Close one eye for six days. Then record from cells in its visual cortex, one at a time. The closed eye can now drive only a fraction of the cells it drove before. Now close both eyes instead. The harm is far smaller. Why would two closed eyes do less harm than one?

scenes.tts: Here is how that is measured. A fine electrode sits next to one cortical cell and records its spikes. A bar of light is shown to one eye, then the other. Each cell goes into one of seven groups. Group one answers only to one eye. Group seven answers only to the other eye. Group four answers about equally to both. Count the cells in each group, and a normal cat gives a hump, with most cells in the middle groups.
scenes.visual: electrode and eyes light one cell; histogram slots 1 to 7 appear, groups named, bars grow into a hump

Count the cells in each group, and a normal cat gives a hump, with most cells in the middle groups.

scenes.tts: Now shut one eye of a young kitten for six days. The closed eye can drive only a fraction of the cells it drove before. Most of the histogram moves toward the open eye. We call this a shift in ocular dominance. A closure from birth for about three months left very few cells that the closed eye could drive. Yet its retina still responded.
scenes.visual: hump bars slide toward the open eye end
scenes.narration: Now shut one eye of a young kitten for six days. The closed eye can drive only a fraction of the cells it drove before. Most of the histogram moves toward the open eye. We call this a shift in ocular dominance. A closure from birth for about three months left very few cells that the closed eye could drive. Yet its retina still responded.

scenes.tts: Is this disuse? Try it in kittens. If unused connections simply wither, closing both eyes should cause a large loss of responses to both. It did not. With both eyes shut, many cells still answered to each eye, though some were abnormal or silent. So the open eye is what hurts the closed one. The two eyes compete for the same cortex, and the more active eye takes territory from the other.

scenes.tts: Age matters. The same closure in an adult cat, even for months, left the histogram normal. In kittens, sensitivity began near the start of the fourth week. It stayed high for several weeks, then declined through the third month. A window like this, when the brain needs experience, is a critical period or a sensitive period. Critical periods begin and end abruptly. Sensitive periods rise and fall gradually. Real windows often fall between.

scenes.tts: This idea helps explain amblyopia. One eye sees poorly because the two eyes gave the young brain unequal input. Glasses alone do not fix it. The treatment follows from competition. Cover the good eye with a patch, so the weak eye is the more active one. It works best in young children. Keep the rule: the more active eye wins, most easily when young.
